newsitem.title: USA: Congress may debate stripped-down disaster bill.
newsitem.headline: Congress may debate stripped-down disaster bill.

text.p: Congressional leaders Thursday abandoned efforts to pass a broad disaster aid bill before leaving for a week-long recess and began work on a bare-bones measure providing about $1 billion for weather-ravaged states.

Despite days of talks, House and Senate negotiators have been unable to bridge differences on spending, environmental and other issues that have held up an $8.4 billion measure to aid more than 30 states and fund U.S. peacekeeping operations overseas.

Congress is scheduled to adjourn Friday for a week-long recess and Republican leaders do not want to leave with the aid in limbo. House and Senate leaders are discussing a plan to pull some disaster relief out of the broader bill and vote on it as a separate measure.
Whether that plan will fly is far from clear since any member of Congress could object and torpedo the entire effort.
"We're floating the propsects of a stripped-down bill,' said House Appropriations Committee Chairman Bob Livingston, a Louisiana Republican.

He said he was afraid some states hit by floods, mudslides and other natural disasters might run out of money for relief efforts if Congress did not act quickly. Asked if all Republican leaders were behind his plan, Livingston said: "I'm in the proces of working the process."

Lawmakers still hope to finish work on the main bill early next month. President Clinton has threatened to veto that measure due to a provision that would autmotically keep the government running if Congress and the White House could not agree on needed spending bills.
Massachusetts Democratic Representative Joe Moakley blamed Republicans for delaying the disaster bill, saying they had loaded it down with unrelated provisions to embarrass the White House.
"For my Republican colleagues to consider going away for Memorial Day when these people are waiting for their flood relief money, which absolutely nobody opposes, is disgraceful," Moakley said.

The legislation contains $5.5 billion to aid more than 30 states hit by floods, mudslides and harsh weather. It provides about $2 billion for U.S. peacekeeping operations in Bosnia and continued U.S. military flights in the Gulf.
One big hurdle is a provision to fund federal programmes at 100 percent of current levels next year if Congress and the White House could not agree on spending bills.

White House officials argue the plan would provide $18 billion less for domestic spending than Republicans agreed to as part of a new balanced budget deal. They also say it would take the pressure off Congress to compromise on spending.

Republican leaders are eager to avoid a repeat of two unpopular government shutdowns during fiscal 1996, which voters blamed on their party. They profess amazement that Clinton would be willing to risk another shutdown.
The White House is adamantly opposed to a proposal by Senate Appropriations Committee Chair Ted Stevens making it easier to build roads on federal lands in Alaska.

The administration said the Alaska Republican's plan could allow roads in pristine areas all over the state. Stevens argues western states need better transportation systems to spur economic development.

Another big dispute is a plan barring the government from spending money on sampling or other statistical techniques for the 2000 census. The administration says sampling could provide a more accurate count of minorities.
